message.content:
The first Studio Ghibli feature to capture Japan’s top honor—the **Japan Academy Film Prize for Picture of the Year**—was **“Princess Mononoke” (1997)**.  
At the 21st Japan Academy Awards (held in 1998) “Princess Mononoke” took home the coveted Picture Award, cementing its status as a landmark Japanese film.

### Box‑office impact on Ghibli’s global standing  

| Aspect | Domestic (Japan) | International ripple |
|--------|------------------|----------------------|
| **Domestic earnings** | Roughly ¥5.9 billion ($55–60 million) – one of the highest‑grossing Japanese movies of the decade. | The record‑breaking ticket sales demonstrated that a fully animated, original story could compete with Hollywood blockbusters in Japan. |
| **Critical reception** | Won Picture of the Year, plus several other Japan Academy Awards (Best Director, Best Screenplay, etc.). | The accolades translated into credibility abroad; distributors saw Ghibli as a serious, award‑winning studio rather than just a niche art house. |
| **Distribution deals** | The film’s success prompted Toho to push for broader theatrical releases across Japan, including limited screenings in major cities outside Tokyo. | In the U.S., the film was released theatrically in 1999 (by Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment) and later on VHS/DVD, sparking interest among American audiences. European distributors followed suit, releasing the film in France, Germany, Italy, and the UK. |
| **Brand visibility** | “Princess Mononoke” became a cultural touchstone; merchandise, theme park attractions, and fan conventions grew around it. | The film’s popularity abroad led to the creation of localized marketing campaigns, subtitled/dubbed releases, and eventually the establishment of a dedicated Ghibli distribution arm (Studio Ghibli USA, later Ghibli Distribution). |
| **Long‑term effect** | The financial success proved that Ghibli could sustain high production values without relying on external funding. | It paved the way for future international co‑production agreements (e.g., “Howl’s Moving Castle” with Disney, “The Tale of the Princess Kaguya” with Netflix). |

In short, **“Princess Mononoke”’s box‑office triumph and prestigious award haul gave Studio Ghibli the leverage to negotiate better overseas distribution contracts, broaden its audience beyond Japan, and establish itself as a globally respected animation powerhouse.** This momentum carried forward into the 2000s, culminating in “Spirited Away” winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature and further solidifying Ghibli’s international reputation.
